claims.claim_vi: MDN describes CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability; also called the CIA triad or AIC triad) as a model that guides an organization's policies for information security.
claims.verified_by: Read from a sparse clone of mdn/content at commit a1aa79c09717761fc72c20bac94bb9c430ed487a on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: The plain-word definitions of confidentiality (only authorised people can read), integrity (a change is detected) and availability (authorised people can use it when needed), and the three examples (a payroll sheet leaking, 'Pay Bob 100 USD' changed to '900 USD', a payment page that does not open), are the author's own wording and illustrative scenarios, not reported incidents.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a definition. The MDN page names the three terms but does not define them, and standards-body texts (NIST, ISO, Internet specifications) were not reachable.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP Security Terminology says encryption has the purpose of confidentiality (only authorised parties with the key can read the data), hashing has the purpose of integrity (a small change in the input gives a completely different hash), digital signatures have the purposes of authenticity and non-repudiation, and authorization occurs after successful authentication.
claims.section: Đọc hình: Bí mật, Toàn vẹn, Khung 2
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of OWASP/CheatSheetSeries at commit f9a631ec47a5fd134bb83b57ce690d7946360cea on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP Threat Modeling cheat sheet gives a STRIDE table that lists the security attribute each category violates: Tampering violates Integrity, Information Disclosure violates Confidentiality, Denial of Service violates Availability, Spoofing violates Authentication, Repudiation violates Accounting, Elevation of Privileges violates Authorization. MDN's STRIDE description gives, for Repudiation, the example of a user deleting data with no deletion audit trail (the basis for 'cần nhật ký ghi vết').

claims.claim_vi: MDN describes Denial of Service as a category of network attack that consumes available server resources, typically by flooding the server with requests, so that the server is sluggish or unavailable for legitimate users.
claims.verified_by: Read from a sparse clone of mdn/content at commit a1aa79c09717761fc72c20bac94bb9c430ed487a on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP Denial of Service cheat sheet says availability is a basic part of the CIA triad and lists measures: rate limiting, request-read timeouts to mitigate slow HTTP attacks, an absolute connection timeout, and avoiding single points of failure with stateless components and redundant systems. It says session (protocol) attacks consume server resources or those of intermediary equipment like firewalls and load-balancers, that a slow HTTP attack makes the server reach its maximum concurrent connection pool, that a minimum data rate set too high can reject legitimate slow clients, and that failure points can range from programming errors to resource exhaustion.

claims.claim_vi: MDN describes a firewall as a system that filters network traffic, letting it pass or blocking it according to specified rules (for example blocking incoming connections aimed at a certain port), and says it can be a single piece of software or a dedicated machine.

claims.claim_vi: That a firewall 'reduces the ways in' is the author's reasoning: MDN's example of blocking incoming connections to a port, combined with the OWASP Attack Surface definition (all the different points where an attacker could get into a system). Neither page states the conclusion.

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP Authentication cheat sheet calls account lockout the most common protection against automated guessing attacks (brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying), says care must be taken so it cannot be used to cause denial of service by locking out other users' accounts, and says these defences often do not give complete protection but a number of them in a defence-in-depth approach can reach a reasonable level. The OWASP STRIDE table's Denial of Service example is an attacker locking a legitimate user out with many failed authentication attempts.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of OWASP/CheatSheetSeries at commit f9a631ec47a5fd134bb83b57ce690d7946360cea on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP Authorization cheat sheet says to implement defence in depth and not depend on any single framework, library, technology or control as the sole thing enforcing access control, and that exploiting authorization flaws lets attackers read, create, modify or delete protected resources, jeopardising their confidentiality, integrity and/or availability. MDN's Web Security page says there is a many-to-many relationship between attacks and defences, so that a single defence can protect against several attacks and defending against one attack may need several defences, giving defence in depth.

claims.claim_vi: MDN says phishing is a social engineering attack: it does not target vulnerabilities in software or hardware but targets users, the target site is not involved in the attack, and the only defence MDN calls really effective is using passkeys instead of passwords.

claims.claim_vi: MDN names STRIDE (security) and LINDDUN (privacy) as two threat-analysis frameworks that give structure to threat modelling by offering threat categories; the OWASP ASVS README describes the project as providing an open application security standard for web apps and web services, defining a comprehensive set of security requirements for designing, developing and testing them. The source's frameworks section has no text, and no other framework is named in the lesson.
claims.verified_by: Read from a sparse clone of mdn/content at commit a1aa79c09717761fc72c20bac94bb9c430ed487a on 2026-10-18. claims.claim_vi: The glossary expands STRIDE and LINDDUN from MDN's category lists, in MDN's order: STRIDE is Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of privilege; LINDDUN is Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance (privacy threats). MDN says each letter of the acronym stands for one category (six for STRIDE, seven for LINDDUN). The OWASP Threat Modeling cheat sheet calls STRIDE a threat modeling technique and mnemonic and lists the same six categories as S, T, R, I, D, E. The glossary shows the first word of each category so that the initials give the abbreviation, and gives the full category name in the explanation.
claims.verified_by: The MDN frameworks page was fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at commit a1aa79c09717761fc72c20bac94bb9c430ed487a on 2026-10-19 and its STRIDE and LINDDUN bullet lists read; the OWASP Threat Modeling cheat sheet was read at commit f9a631ec47a5fd134bb83b57ce690d7946360cea (the STRIDE table). The MDN page never writes the expansions in one sentence; the expansion is read off the category lists, whose order matches the letters.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP Password Storage says stored passwords must be protected from an attacker even if the application or database is compromised, that they should be hashed with a strong slow algorithm rather than stored in plain text, and that hashing is one-way so an attacker who obtains the hash cannot use it to log in as the victim. Details of password storage are in the sibling lesson sd-14-003.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of OWASP/CheatSheetSeries at commit f9a631ec47a5fd134bb83b57ce690d7946360cea on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: The cryptography library documents HMAC as a message authentication code built from a hash function and a secret key that can verify both the integrity and authenticity of a message (the key must be kept secret), and documents authenticated encryption (AEAD, including AES-GCM) as providing both confidentiality and integrity, with decrypt raising InvalidTag when the tag does not validate. It documents CTR as turning a block cipher into a stream cipher. OWASP Cryptographic Storage says authenticated modes (GCM, CCM) give integrity and authenticity as well as confidentiality, while CTR and CBC give no guarantee about authenticity and need separate authentication.

claims.claim_vi: Observed (experiment 1A): a plain SHA-256 hash sent next to 'Pay Bob 100 USD' did not match after a one-bit accidental change with the old hash kept (check failed), but a check passed when the attacker replaced both the message ('Pay Bob 900 USD') and the hash with its own SHA-256.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running exp_cia_ic.py on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18 (Python 3.13.16, cryptography 50.0.1, throw-away random keys, no network).

claims.claim_vi: Observed (experiment 1B): with HMAC-SHA256 and a secret 32-byte key, the genuine message and tag verified; the forged message with the old tag did not; the forged message with a tag the attacker computed with a guessed key did not; the message stayed readable.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running exp_cia_ic.py on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18 (Python 3.13.16, cryptography 50.0.1, throw-away random keys, no network).

claims.claim_vi: Observed (experiment 1C): AES-256-CTR ciphertext of the 15-byte message was 15 bytes and did not contain 'Bob'; flipping one ciphertext bit at index 8 (0x31 '1' to 0x39 '9') made decryption succeed without any error and return 'Pay Bob 900 USD'. Why the flipped bit appears at the same place in the plaintext (CTR behaves as a stream cipher) is the author's general knowledge beyond the observation and the library doc that CTR turns a block cipher into a stream cipher.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running exp_cia_ic.py on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18 (Python 3.13.16, cryptography 50.0.1, throw-away random keys, no network).

claims.claim_vi: Observed (experiment 1D): AES-256-GCM ciphertext was 31 bytes (15 bytes of message plus a 16-byte tag), did not contain 'Bob', decrypted the untouched ciphertext to 'Pay Bob 100 USD', and with the same bit flipped decrypt raised InvalidTag and returned nothing.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running exp_cia_ic.py on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18 (Python 3.13.16, cryptography 50.0.1, throw-away random keys, no network).

claims.claim_vi: The Python socketserver documentation says TCPServer and its sibling classes process requests synchronously (each request must be completed before the next can start), that this is unsuitable when a request takes long or the client is slow, and that ThreadingMixIn and ForkingMixIn give asynchronous behaviour with a thread or process per request.
claims.verified_by: Read from a file fetched from python/cpython at commit cdf010b10c673e1ec4faaf3f8f9be39237986880 on 2026-10-18.

claims.claim_vi: Observed (experiment 2): with 0 idle clients, 5 of 5 normal clients got an answer in under 0.01 s from all three servers. With 3 idle clients connected first (connected, never sent a line): server A (one request at a time, no read limit) answered 0 of 5 within 5 s; server B (one at a time, 1.0 s read timeout) answered 5 of 5 after 2.70 s; server C (thread per connection) answered 5 of 5 in under 0.01 s.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running exp_availability.py on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18 (Python 3.13.16, 127.0.0.1 only, ports chosen by the OS; two runs gave the same counts and the same 2.70 s for server B).

claims.claim_vi: That B's 2.70 s equals 3 x 1.0 s minus the 0.3 s the script waited before the normal clients started is the author's reading of the script's constants; experiment 2 is a toy model of one cause (the only worker held by idle connections), does not measure a flood, and does not measure the limit of server C's threads or connections (OWASP only says a slow HTTP attack can reach the maximum concurrent connection pool).
claims.verified_by: Author's inference from exp_availability.py constants (SLOW = 3, B_TIMEOUT = 1.0, sleep 0.3 s); the limit of server C was not tested.

design_notes_vi: Hai khung xếp dọc: ba thẻ cho ba điều cần giữ (mỗi thẻ một ví dụ khi hỏng), rồi năm ghi chú nối biện pháp với điều nó giữ và nhắc xếp nhiều lớp. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source body has five headings but text only under Basic Defense Mechanisms; the lesson fills the empty Introduction, CIA triad, threats and frameworks parts from sources it read and labels the plain-word definitions as general knowledge.
The source calls a firewall a network security device; MDN says it can be a single piece of software or a dedicated machine, and the lesson follows MDN.

The source says encryption converts information into a code to prevent unauthorized access; the lesson adds that encryption alone does not detect modification (AES-CTR accepted a flipped bit, AES-GCM rejected it) and that this is why integrity needs its own control.

The source says antivirus software detects and removes malware without stating limits; the lesson cites OWASP that anti-malware solutions cannot be 100% effective and should be an additional layer, and gives no detection rate.

The source's three defence mechanisms include none whose main purpose is integrity or availability; the lesson adds message authentication codes, digital signatures, rate limits, timeouts and redundancy and says this pairing is the author's own.
The source's frameworks section has no text; the lesson names only STRIDE and LINDDUN (MDN) and OWASP ASVS (its own README) and enumerates no other framework.
